text: Friction. Real objects interact with their surroundings, which means the environment can cause a resistance, a force of friction. Friction opposes relative motion between systems in contact, but also allows us to move. Try walking on ice. You need boots that grip, that is, increase friction. Friction is one of the common contact forces introduced in chapter 5. In this chapter, we use friction quantitatively by adding it to the free body diagram and applying Newton's second law. Static and kinetic friction. Friction. Friction is a force that opposes relative motion between systems in contact. There are several forms of friction. Sliding friction, F sub S, is parallel to the contact surface between systems and is always in a direction that opposes motion or attempted motion of the systems relative to each other. Kinetic friction, F sub K, is when two systems are in contact and moving relative to one another. For example, friction slows a hockey puck sliding on ice. When the static friction is greater than the kinetic friction, F sub S is greater than F sub K, the objects are stationary. Static and kinetic friction. If two systems are in contact and stationary relative to one another, then the friction between them is called static friction. If two systems are in contact and moving relative to one another, then the friction between them is called kinetic friction. See the Flipping Physics video on the course webpage. This video reviews how friction fits into Newton's second law. Watch for the difference between a friction model and a free body diagram. Friction is one force included in some vector F, not a separate shortcut. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If an object does not move when pushed, does that mean friction is zero or that static friction has adjusted to match the push? Consider trying to slide a heavy crate across a concrete floor. You might push very hard and not move the crate at all. This means the static friction responds to what you do. It increases in the opposite direction to resist your push. Once in motion, it is easier to keep it in motion than it was to get it started, which indicates that the kinetic friction is less than the static friction. If you add mass to the crate, you need to push even harder to get it started and also to keep it moving. If you oiled the concrete, you would find it easier to get the crate started and keep it going. Figure is a pictorial representation of how friction occurs at the interface between two objects. Close up inspection of these surfaces reveal them to be rough. Thus, when you push to get an object moving, you must raise the object until it can skip along with just the tips of the surface hitting, breaking off the points or both. A considerable force can be resisted by friction with no apparent motion. The harder the surfaces are pushed together, the more force is needed to move them. Part of the friction is due to adhesive forces between surface molecules of the two objects, which explains the dependence on the surface composition. Adhesion varies with substances in contact and is a complicated aspect of surface physics. Once an object is moving, there are fewer points of contact, that is, fewer molecules adhering, so less force is required to keep the object moving. At small but non-zero speeds, friction is nearly independent of speed. The magnitude of the frictional force has two forms, static and kinetic. The models of each are empirical, experimentally determined, and they are not vector equations. Magnitude of static and kinetic friction. The magnitude of static friction, F sub S, is F sub S is less than or equal to mu sub S N, where mu sub S, or mu sub S, is the coefficient of static friction, and N is the magnitude of the normal force N. Static friction is a responsive force that increases to be equal and opposite to whatever force is exerted. Once the applied force exceeds F sub S maximum, the object moves, and F sub S maximum equals mu sub S N. The magnitude of kinetic friction, F sub K, is given by F sub K equals mu sub K N, where mu sub K, or mu sub K, is the coefficient of kinetic friction. Figure illustrates the transition from static friction, stationary, in figure A, to kinetic friction, moving in figure B. The coefficients of kinetic friction are less than their static counterparts. The values of mu provide only an approximate description of the friction given. Table. Approximate coefficients of static and kinetic friction, refer to the course notes for the full entries. In both static and kinetic frictions, the equation depends on the materials through mu sub S, or mu sub K, and the normal force. The direction of friction is always opposite to the direction of motion, parallel to the surface between objects, and perpendicular to the normal force. For example, if the crate you try to push has a mass of 100 kilograms, then the normal force is equal to its weight. W equals mg equals 100 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared, equals 981 newtons perpendicular to the floor. If the coefficient of static friction is 0.45, you would have to exert a force parallel to the floor that is greater than F sub S maximum, equals mu sub S times N, equals 0.45 times 981 newtons, equals 440 newtons to move the crate. Once there's motion, friction is less, and the coefficient of kinetic friction might be 0.30, so that a force of only F sub K equals mu sub K times N, equals 0.30 times 981 newtons, equals 290 newtons, keeps it moving at a constant speed. If the floor is lubricated, both coefficients are considerably less than otherwise. The coefficient of friction is a unitless quantity, with a magnitude between 0 and 1.0. The actual value depends on the two surfaces in contact. The equations for static and kinetic friction are empirical laws that describe the behavior of the frictional force. While these formulas are useful for practical purposes, they are not general principles, for example, Newton's second law. There are cases for which these equations are not even good approximations. For example, neither formula is accurate for lubricated surfaces or surfaces sliding at high speeds. Example problem, static and kinetic friction. The problem, a 20 kilogram crate is at rest on a floor as shown in figure. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and floor is 0.70, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.60. A horizontal force vector p is applied to the crate. Find the force of friction if a vector p equals 20 newtons i hat, b vector p equals 30 newtons i hat, c vector p equals 120 newtons i hat, and d vector p equals 180 newtons i hat. The worked solution follows. The model. The crate is modeled as a particle on a horizontal floor. We choose plus i hat to point to the right and plus j hat upward. The applied force points in the plus i hat direction, and friction points in the minus i hat direction because it opposes impending or actual motion. The normal force points in the plus j hat direction, and the weight points in the minus j hat direction. Static friction adjusts up to its maximum value. If the applied force exceeds that maximum, the crate slides, and kinetic friction acts. The math. The vertical force is balanced because the crate has no vertical acceleration. Newton's second law in the vertical direction gives some f sub y equals 0, n minus mg equals 0, n equals mg. The maximum static and kinetic friction magnitudes are determined by the normal force. F sub s maximum equals mu sub s n. F sub k equals mu sub k n. The shared normal and friction thresholds are determined before evaluating each applied force. n equals 20.0 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared, which equals 196 newtons. F sub s maximum equals 0.70 times 196 newtons, which equals 1.4 times 10 to the second newtons. F sub k equals 0.60 times 196 newtons, which equals 1.2 times 10 to the second newtons. For applied forces below F sub s maximum, the crate remains at rest, and static friction matches the applied force. For applied forces above F sub s maximum, the crate slips and the friction is kinetic. Part A. First, we evaluate P equals 20 newtons. Since 20 newtons is less than 1.4 times 10 to the second newtons, static friction matches the applied force. F equals 20 newtons. Part B. Next, we evaluate P equals 30 newtons. Since 30 newtons is less than 1.4 times 10 to the second newtons, static friction matches the applied force. F equals 30 newtons. Part C. Then we evaluate P equals 120 newtons. Since 120 newtons is less than 1.4 times 10 to the second newtons, static friction still matches the applied force. F equals 120 newtons. Part D. Finally, we evaluate P equals 180 newtons. Since 180 newtons is greater than 1.4 times 10 to the second newtons, the crate slips and kinetic friction acts. F equals F sub K, which equals 1.2 times 10 to the second newtons. The conclusion. For applied forces of 20 newtons, 30 newtons, and 120 newtons, static friction keeps the crate at rest and equals the applied force in magnitude. For an applied force of 180 newtons, static friction is not large enough, so the crate slides and the friction force has kinetic magnitude 1.2 times 10 to the two newtons. In each case, the friction force points opposite vector P. Friction and the incline plane. Friction plays an obvious role when there is an object on a slope. It could be a crate pushed up a ramp or a skateboarder coasting down a mountain, but the basic physics is the same. Inclined problems are easier when the axes are rotated so that one axis is parallel to the slope and the other is perpendicular to it. This uses the same component logic from chapter 2 and extends the incline free body diagram from chapter 5. We generalize the sloping surface and call it an incline plane. Recall the weight on an incline problem where we orient our system axes so that the motion is along the x-axis only, meaning flat in the transformed coordinate system. When an object rests on a horizontal surface, the normal force supporting it is equal in magnitude to its weight. Additionally, simple friction is always proportional to the normal force. However, with the incline plane, we must find the force acting on the object that is directed perpendicular to the surface, meaning it is a component of the weight. Consider an object that slides down an incline plane at constant velocity, meaning the net force is zero. Such conditions can be used to measure the coefficient of kinetic friction between two objects. Recall the free body diagram from chapter 5 where we found that w sub x equals w sine theta and the friction opposes the motion along the x-axis. The normal force opposes the weight along the y-axis or n equals w cosine theta. Therefore, the kinetic friction on a slope is f sub k equals mu sub k n, which equals mu sub k mg cosine theta. Writing this out in terms of forces, we have the sum of f sub x equals f sub k minus w sub x equals zero. So f sub k equals w sub x and mu sub k mg cosine theta equals mg sine theta. Now we can solve for mu sub k. Mu sub k equals mg sine theta divided by mg cosine theta, which equals tangent theta. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. On an incline, why is the normal force smaller than mg, even though the object still has its full weight? A dot physics video is linked on the course webpage. This video shows three experiments you can do to measure the coefficient of friction. Skip to six minutes and 44 seconds to see the experiment with an incline plane. Example problem. Downhill skier. The problem. A skier with a mass of 62 kilograms is sliding down a snowy slope at a constant acceleration. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction for the skier if the friction force is known to be 45.0 newtons. The worked solution follows. The model. The skier is modeled as a particle sliding down a rigid incline. We choose plus i hat to point down the slope and plus j hat to point perpendicular to the surface away from the surface. The kinetic friction force points up the slope in the minus i hat direction because it opposes the skier's motion. The normal force points in the plus j hat direction and the weight points vertically downward. The skier remains in contact with the slope so the acceleration perpendicular to the surface is zero. The figure gives the incline angle as 25 degrees. The math. The coefficient of kinetic friction is determined from the relationship between kinetic friction and the normal force f sub k equals mu sub k n. The normal force comes from the force balance perpendicular to the slope. The perpendicular component of the skier's weight points into the slope so Newton's second law perpendicular to the slope gives some f sub y equals zero. Newton's minus mg cosine theta equals zero n equals mg cosine theta. We substitute this expression for n into the kinetic friction equation and solve for mu sub k. f sub k equals mu sub k mg cosine theta. mu sub k equals f sub k over mg cosine theta. The coefficient of kinetic friction follows from the ratio of the measured friction force to the normal force. mu sub k equals 45.0 Newton's over 62 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared cosine 25 degrees equals 0.082. The conclusion. The coefficient of kinetic friction for the skier is mu sub k equals 0.082. This value is reasonable for sliding on snow and is smaller than many dry surface friction coefficients. Atomic scale explanations of friction. The simpler aspects of friction rely on its macroscopic or large scale characteristics. Researchers are finding that the atomic nature of friction also has several fundamental microscopic or small scale characteristics. These characteristics hold the potential for the development of nearly frictionless environments that helps reduce mechanical wear and energy loss due to heat. So far, we have noted that friction is proportional to the normal force but not to the amount of area in contact. When two rough surfaces are in contact, the actual contact area is a tiny fraction of the total area because only high spots touch. When a greater normal force is exerted, the actual contact area increases and we find that the friction is proportional to this area as illustrated by the figure on the course web page. The atomic scale seeks to explain why do surfaces get warmer when rubbed? Essentially, atoms are linked with one another to form lattices. When surfaces rub, the surface atoms adhere and cause atomic lattices to vibrate, meaning they create sound waves. The sound waves diminish with distance and their energy is converted to heat. Chemical reactions related to frictional wear can also occur between atoms and surfaces. The figure on the course web page shows how the tip of a probe drawn across another material is deformed by atomic scale friction. The force needed to drag the tip can be measured and is related to shear stress. The variation in shear stress is more than a factor of 10 to the 12th and difficult to predict theoretically. Checkpoint, pause and check your understanding. Why can friction depend on the normal force even though the apparent contact area looks unchanged? An efficient engineer video is linked on the course web page. This video reviews friction in mechanical systems. Use it as a way to connect the abstract ideas to physical systems and components. Example problem, sliding blocks. The problem, the two blocks shown in the figure on the course web page are attached to each other by a massless string that is wrapped around a frictionless pulley. When the bottom 4.0 kilograms block is pulled to the left by the constant force vector p, the top 2.0 kilograms block slides across it to the right. Find the magnitude of the force necessary to move the blocks at constant speed. Assume that the coefficient of kinetic friction between all surfaces is 0.40. The worked solution follows. The model. Each block is modeled as a particle. We choose plus i hat to point to the right and plus j hat upward. The top block moves to the right at constant speed, so the tension on it points in the plus i hat direction and kinetic friction from the lower block points in the minus i hat direction. The lower block moves to the left at constant speed, so the applied force vector p points in the minus i hat direction. The tension friction from the top block and friction from the floor all point in the plus i hat direction on the lower block. Both blocks have zero acceleration. The math. For the top block, constant speed requires zero net force in both directions. The normal force from the lower block balances the weight of the top block and the tension balances kinetic friction. Some f sub x equals zero. Some f sub y equals zero. T minus mu sub k and sub 1 equals zero. N sub 1 minus m sub 1 g equals zero. We solve these equations for n sub 1 and T. N sub 1 equals m sub 1 g. T equals mu sub k and sub 1 equals mu sub k m sub 1 g. For the lower block, constant speed also requires zero net force. The floor normal force must support the lower block and the downward normal force from the upper block. Some f sub y equals zero. N sub 2 minus m sub 2 g minus n sub 1 equals zero. N sub 2 equals m sub 2 g plus n sub 1. The horizontal forces on the lower block are the applied force to the left and three forces to the right. Tension, friction from the top block and friction from the floor. Newton's second law in the horizontal direction gives some f sub x equals zero. T plus mu sub k and sub 1 plus mu sub k and sub 2 minus p equals zero. P equals T plus mu sub k m sub 1 g plus mu sub k m sub 1 g plus mu sub k times the quantity m sub 2 g plus m sub 1 g equals mu sub k g times the quantity 3 m sub 1 plus m sub 2. The required applied force follows from the horizontal force balance on the lower block. P equals 0.400 times 9.81 meters per second squared times the quantity 3 times 2.00 kilograms plus 4.00 kilograms equals 39.2 newtons. The conclusion. The applied force needed to move the blocks at constant speed is p equals 39.2 newtons. This force balances the tension and both kinetic friction forces acting to the right on the lower block so the lower block can move left with zero acceleration. Example problem. Crate on an accelerating truck. The problem. A 50 kilogram crate rests on the bed of a truck as shown in figure. The coefficients of friction between the surfaces are mu sub k equals 0.30 and mu sub s equals 0.40. Find the frictional force on the crate when the truck is accelerating forward relative to the ground at a 2.0 meters per second squared and b 5.0 meters per second squared. The worked solution follows. The model. The crate is modeled as a particle on the horizontal bed of the truck. We choose plus i hat to point forward with the truck and plus j hat upward. The weight points in the negative j hat direction and the normal force points in the plus j hat direction. The friction force on the crate points forward in the plus i hat direction because the truck bed tends to slide forward underneath the crate. If static friction can provide the required acceleration, the crate does not slip. If not, the crate slips backward relative to the truck and kinetic friction acts forward on the crate. The math. The vertical force is balanced because the crate has no vertical acceleration. Newton's second law in the vertical direction gives some f sub y equals 0. N minus mg equals 0. N equals mg. The largest possible static friction and the kinetic friction magnitude are f sub s maximum equals mu sub s n. f sub k equals mu sub k n. The normal force sets the maximum static friction and the kinetic friction magnitude. N equals 50.0 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared, which equals 491 newtons. f sub s maximum equals 0.400 times 491 newtons equals 196 newtons. f sub k equals 0.300 times 491 newtons equals 147 newtons. Part a. First, we evaluate the truck acceleration a equals 2.00 meters per second squared. If the crate does not slip, static friction must provide the crate's horizontal acceleration. f sub s equals ma, which equals 50.0 kilograms times 2.00 meters per second squared and equals 100 newtons. Since 100 newtons is less than 196 newtons, static friction is sufficient and the crate does not slip. Part b. Next, we evaluate the truck acceleration a equals 5.00 meters per second squared. If the crate were to move with the truck, the required static friction would be f sub s equals ma, which equals 50.0 kilograms times 5.00 meters per second squared and equals 250 newtons. Since 250 newtons is greater than 196 newtons, static friction is not sufficient and the crate slips. The frictional force on the crate is therefore kinetic. f equals f sub k, which equals 147 newtons. The conclusion. For a truck acceleration of 2.00 meters per second squared, static friction acts forward on the crate with magnitude 100 newtons and prevents slipping. For a truck acceleration of 5.00 meters per second squared, the required static friction exceeds the maximum possible value. So the crate slips and kinetic friction acts forward with magnitude 147 newtons. Example problem. Snowboarding. The problem. Earlier, we analyzed the situation of a downhill skier moving at constant velocity to determine the coefficient of kinetic friction. Now, let's do a similar analysis to determine acceleration. The snowboarder of figure glides down a slope that is inclined at 13 degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the board and the snow is mu sub k equals 0.20. What is the acceleration of the snowboarder? The worked solution follows. The model. The snowboarder is modeled as a particle sliding down a rigid incline. We choose plus i hat to point downhill along the slope and plus j hat to point perpendicular to the slope away from the surface. The component of weight parallel to the slope points in the plus i hat direction. Kinetic friction points uphill in the minus i hat direction. The normal force points in the plus j hat direction and the perpendicular component of the weight points in the minus j hat direction. Air resistance is neglected. The math. The snowboarder accelerates along the slope while the perpendicular acceleration is zero. The force's parallel to the slope are the downhill component of weight and the uphill kinetic friction force. The forces perpendicular to the slope are the normal force and the perpendicular component of weight. Newton's second law gives sum f sub x equals m a sub x sum f sub y equals zero. Resolving the forces along the chosen axes gives m g sine theta minus f sub k equals m a sub x. Newton's minus m g cosine theta equals zero. The perpendicular equation determines the normal force and kinetic friction depends on that normal force. N equals m g cosine theta. F sub k equals mu sub k n equals mu sub k m g cosine theta. We substitute the kinetic friction expression into the parallel force equation and solve for the acceleration. M g sine theta minus mu sub k m g cosine theta equals m a sub x. A sub x equals g times sine theta minus mu sub k cosine theta. The downhill acceleration follows from the balance between the downhill gravity component and uphill kinetic friction. A sub x equals 9.81 meters per second squared times sine 13 degrees minus 0.20 cosine 13 degrees equals 0.29 meters per second squared. The conclusion. The snowboarder accelerates downhill at 0.29 meters per second squared. The acceleration is small because the downhill gravity component is only slightly larger than the kinetic friction force opposing the motion.

Atomic scale explanations of friction. The simpler aspects of friction rely on its macroscopic or
large scale characteristics. Researchers are finding that the atomic nature of friction also has
several fundamental microscopic or small scale characteristics. These characteristics hold the
potential for the development of nearly frictionless environments that helps reduce mechanical
wear and energy loss due to heat. So far, we have noted that friction is proportional to the
normal force but not to the amount of area in contact. When two rough surfaces are in contact,
the actual contact area is a tiny fraction of the total area because only high spots touch.
When a greater normal force is exerted, the actual contact area increases and we find that the
friction is proportional to this area as illustrated by the figure on the course web page.
The atomic scale seeks to explain why do surfaces get warmer when rubbed? Essentially,
atoms are linked with one another to form lattices. When surfaces rub, the surface atoms adhere and
cause atomic lattices to vibrate, meaning they create sound waves. The sound waves diminish with
distance and their energy is converted to heat. Chemical reactions related to frictional wear can
also occur between atoms and surfaces. The figure on the course web page shows how the tip of a
probe drawn across another material is deformed by atomic scale friction. The force needed to drag
the tip can be measured and is related to shear stress. The variation in shear stress is more
than a factor of 10 to the 12th and difficult to predict theoretically. Checkpoint, pause and check
